---
title: Write a plugin with the AI
description: Ask the agent in the app to write a PLUGIN.md plugin with you. It reads the language reference, validates the draft, dry-runs read tools against the live service, and opens the usual review sheet so you decide whether to install.
icon: Sparkles
---

A plugin is just text, so the agent in the app can write one with you. Ask for "a plugin for the
gym booking site" and you end up with a `PLUGIN.md` folder to review and install. The agent works
through the tools of the built-in **Plugins** plugin (`plugins`), and it can't install anything
without you.

## The tools

| Tool | Effect | Does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `plugins.reference` | read | The plugin language on one page: manifest, steps, expressions, stdlib, abilities, limits and an example. The agent reads it on demand before writing or editing a plugin; it is not in every prompt. |
| `plugins.validate` | read | Validates a draft folder (`{ files: { "PLUGIN.md": "…", "tools/x.yaml": "…" } }`) with the same loader as the app. Returns `{ ok: true, id, version, tools, widgets, campus, network, abilities }` or `{ ok: false, issues }` with the file and step of each problem. |
| `plugins.tryTool` | read | Runs one **read** tool of a draft for real, without installing it: live requests, your campus sessions for the services the draft declares, a throwaway store. Write, money and public tools can't be tried. Results are untrusted data. |
| `plugins.source` | read | The files of an installed plugin document, to explain, fix or fork it. Built-in TypeScript plugins have no document. |
| `plugins.install` | write | Opens the app's review sheet for a link (GitHub folder or `PLUGIN.md` URL) or a draft (`{ files }`). It only opens the sheet: you decide there. |

By default the Plugins plugin asks before running `write` tools, so unless you changed that mode,
the agent also checks with you before it opens the sheet.

## The flow

<Steps>
<Step>

### Describe what you want

Say what the plugin should do and, if you know it, which page or API it should use. If it's a
campus service, say so: the plugin will call it with your signed-in session and never sees your
password.

</Step>
<Step>

### The agent drafts and validates

It reads `plugins.reference`, writes `PLUGIN.md` and the tool files, and keeps calling
`plugins.validate` until no issues are left.

</Step>
<Step>

### It tries the read tools

`plugins.tryTool` runs a read tool against the real service, so you see actual results before
anything is installed.

</Step>
<Step>

### You review and install

`plugins.install` opens the same review sheet as an install link: Official or Community, the
campus services, websites and app features the plugin can reach, and every tool with its effect.
A draft written in chat counts as a community plugin. Nothing is installed until you tap
*Install*.

</Step>
</Steps>

To change an installed document, ask the agent to fix or extend it. It reads the files with
`plugins.source`, edits them, validates, and opens the sheet again with the new version. If you
paste a plugin link in chat, the agent opens the sheet with `plugins.install { link }`.

## Share what you made

The agent's draft is an ordinary plugin folder. To share it, or to keep it updating from a link,
put the folder in a public GitHub repo; the folder URL becomes its install link (see
[Your first plugin](/en/docs/build/quickstart#share-it)). Before you publish, run the
[author CLI](/en/docs/build/declarative-plugins#test) on a computer and add recorded tests.

## Safety

- The agent never installs on its own. `plugins.install` only opens the review sheet.
- `tryTool` runs only read tools, reaches only what the draft declares, and stores nothing.
- An installed draft follows the same rules as any community plugin: `write`, `money` and
  `public` tools ask first, and results reach the AI as data, never as instructions.

The language itself is covered in [Declarative plugins](/en/docs/build/declarative-plugins), and
[Permissions](/en/docs/concepts/permissions) explains how the modes work.
